description:
Oculus Deus is a student engineering team building ATLAS-X, a physics-first planetary base architecture and Split-Twin analog engine.

Soumen Roy (Team Lead & Systems Architect): 37-table planetary database (SQLite/H3), 4-step pipeline integration, 3D orbital visualizer, and mission deck.

Shreesay Saxena (Data & Algorithm Engineer): Core similarity/screening modules, planetary data analysis, and submission documentation.

Hardik Dheer (Team Member): Ideation and general coordination.
summary:
ATLAS-X (Automated Terrestrial & Lunar/Martian Analog System) is a physics-grounded planetary site qualification and terrestrial analog convergence engine. Deep-space exploration faces an operational deadlock: mission scientists select scientifically rich landing sites that spacecraft engineers must reject due to landing hazard envelopes.

ATLAS-X bridges this divide. It combines open data across 524 Moon and Mars sites with 12 under-studied Earth analogs. Candidate sites are first screened against strict engineering safety limits for slope and rock hazards. A four-axis physics engine then scores terrain, mineralogy, temperature, and volatiles, filtering out over-studied locations to pinpoint high-fidelity testing grounds. To protect surface infrastructure, ATLAS-X maps a three-zone hexagonal base layout that shields habitats from rocket exhaust sandblasting, while fuel-cell power sizing saves 8.5 metric tons of lunar night battery mass. Validated against real Apollo and Martian samples across 220 automated tests, ATLAS-X gives mission teams verified, flight-ready site selection.
details:
ATLAS-X: Automated Terrestrial & Lunar/Martian Analog System

Project Overview & The Core Exploration Problem

As space agencies advance the Artemis lunar campaign and plan human architectures for Mars, mission architects face a fundamental operational bottleneck:

  1. The Science vs. Engineering Deadlock: Planetary scientists regularly nominate scientifically rich landing sites (such as crater walls, river deltas, and polar cold traps) that lander engineers must reject due to hazardous landing envelopes: slopes exceeding 10 degrees, boulder fields exceeding 5% surface coverage, and supersonic plume-surface sandblasting.
  2. The "Fake 99%" Analog Flaw: Legacy terrestrial analog selection tools rely on opaque, single-score distance metrics that produce claimed "95% to 99% matches" between Earth and planetary surfaces. These tools ignore non-negotiable physical laws: Earth has an atmosphere, 1.0g gravity, and cannot naturally duplicate the 35 K cryogenic vacuum conditions of Lunar Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs).

ATLAS-X resolves this crisis. Built on an authoritative master database harmonizing open telemetry across 524 candidate landing sites on the Moon and Mars with 12 under-studied terrestrial analogs, ATLAS-X pairs a Tier-1 Hard Engineering Constraint Mask with a decoupled four-axis similarity engine, an Anti-Cliché spatial novelty prior, an explicit 3-Hexagon base topology, and an end-to-end scientific verification audit.

ATLAS-X interactive 3D Mission Control dashboard displaying Uber H3 hexagonal spatial indexing (Resolution 7), real-time engineering safety masks, and cross-planetary candidate site evaluation for the Moon and Mars.

What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

ATLAS-X operates as a four-step Cross-Planetary Convergence Engine that translates multi-agency satellite telemetry into verified mission decisions:

Step 1: Extraterrestrial Landing Site Optimization

Candidate landing zones on the Moon and Mars are filtered and ranked through a two-tier screening process:

  • Tier-1 Hard Safety Cutoffs: Any site that violates critical spacecraft safety limits is immediately eliminated:
    • Surface Slopes over 10 Degrees: Disqualified to prevent lander tip-over at touchdown.
    • Rock Abundance over 5%: Disqualified to prevent lander footpads from striking dangerous boulders.
    • Lunar Solar Illumination under 80% or Earth Visibility under 50%: Disqualified to ensure continuous solar power and direct radio communications without relying on complex relay networks.
    • Martian Atmospheric Deceleration Limit: Disqualified if higher than -2,000 meters elevation or above 55 degrees latitude, guaranteeing enough atmospheric thickness for parachute braking while remaining within reach of subsurface water ice sheets.
  • ISRU Mechanical Traction Energetics: For qualified landing sites, ATLAS-X computes the specific mechanical work (Joules per kilogram) required for an autonomous rover to haul excavated water ice from cryogenic crater traps across sloped terrain:
    Where mechanical traction is integrated across surface gravity, haul distance, rolling resistance, and slope angle. For example, transporting 1 metric ton of ice along a 3.2-kilometer route consumes only 0.17 kilowatt-hours (0.60 MJ) of traction energy, roughly equivalent to running an electric kettle for eight minutes.
  • Tier-2 Multi-Factor Scoring: Sites that pass all hard safety cutoffs are evaluated across multiple criteria (scientific value, proximity to ice, and solar exposure) using smooth S-curve utility scoring regularized by sensor error margins.

Step 2: Terrestrial Screening & Anti-Cliché Discovery

To find genuine Earth analogs, the engine screens candidate locations by removing vegetation and human activity:

  • Biosphere and Vegetation Masking: Satellite infrared vegetation indexing automatically removes forests, grasslands, farmland, and cities.
  • Thermal Inertia Calibration: The system calculates the bedrock-to-sand ratio across deserts using daily satellite temperature swings from day to night.
  • Mineral Spectral Matching: High-resolution Earth imaging spectrometers match hydrated clay and sulfate minerals against Martian hyperspectral absorption signatures.
  • Anti-Cliché Discovery Filter: Analog testing has historically suffered from over-studying a narrow set of familiar sites (Antarctica, the Atacama Desert, Iceland, and Hawaii). ATLAS-X applies an 85% mathematical reduction over these regions to enforce global discovery:
    This mathematical suppression forces the engine to uncover 12 under-studied, high-fidelity global analogs, including the hyper-arid yardangs of the Qaidam Basin, the volcanic subglacial springs of Svalbard, the ultra-acidic brines of the Danakil Depression, and the basaltic impact structures of Lonar Crater.

Step 3: Pure Physics Engine & Cross-Planetary Scaling

  • Decoupled Four-Axis Physical Matching: Instead of compressing planetary environments into a single misleading percentage, ATLAS-X decouples matching across four orthogonal physical axes:
    • Axis A (Terrain and Surface Mechanics): Slope steepness, ruggedness, and boulder hazards.
    • Axis B (Geochemistry and Raw Materials): Iron, titanium, and mineral spectral signatures.
    • Axis C (Thermal Environment): Day-to-night temperature extremes and surface heat retention.
    • Axis D (Atmosphere, Dust, and Water): Water-equivalent hydrogen, permafrost depth, surface wind speeds, and dust deposition rates.
  • Analytic Variance Propagation (Conservative 95% Confidence Bound): Because orbital instruments vary widely in spatial resolution (1 meter per pixel for orbital cameras versus 300 kilometers for gamma-ray spectrometers), measurement variances are propagated via first-order Taylor expansion into a Lower Confidence Bound (LCB):This automatically penalizes sites with high measurement uncertainty, ensuring that top-ranked sites are supported by high-resolution, peer-reviewed data.
  • Dimensionless Cross-Planetary Physics Scaling: Cross-body aeolian dust lifting is scaled between Earth and Mars using the dimensionless Shields parameter:

Step 4: Mission Decision Scorecards

The platform outputs comprehensive mission control scorecards synthesizing base qualifications, primary analog matches, complementary multi-site pairings, ground test chamber requirements (vacuum, gravity cranes, and cryogenic chillers), life-support power sizing, and surface zoning maps.

End-to-end data pipeline from multi-agency open data ingestion (NASA PDS, USGS, ESA, JAXA) through spatial constraint masking, 4-axis decoupled physics matching, and decision scorecard generation.

How Is the Project Creative?

Innovation 1: Decoupled Physics Realism vs. Legacy Single-Score Tools

Legacy analog selection platforms claim 95% to 99% similarity between Earth and extraterrestrial sites by relying on aggregate distance metrics that ignore non-negotiable physical laws:

  • The Reality of Cryogenic PSRs: Earth cannot naturally duplicate the 35 K cryogenic conditions of lunar polar cold traps. On Axis C (Thermophysics), high-latitude Arctic sites achieve an authentic ~1.1% match against lunar PSRs.
    • Surface Gravity Offload: 62.1% active crane offload required for Mars testing; 83.5% offload for Lunar testing.
    • Barometric Pressure Gap: +2.19 log orders of magnitude for Mars; +14.98 log orders for the Moon (requiring vacuum chamber testing).
    • Ionizing Radiation Multiplier: 73.5x higher cosmic radiation on the Moon; 77.9x higher on Mars.
    • Cryogenic Temperature Gap: +125.7 K to +213.8 K (requiring ground thermal-vacuum chillers).
    • Mars Twin Pairing: Danakil Depression (hydrothermal brines and volcanic geology) combined with Bockfjorden Svalbard (cryogenic carbonate alteration) delivers an 80.6% combined system fidelity.
    • Moon Twin Pairing: Pilbara Craton combined with Samail Ophiolite peridotite achieves 61.5% combined system fidelity.

Innovation 2: Settlement Infrastructure & 3-Hexagon Base Topology

Permanent human settlements require functional spatial zoning rather than a single pinpoint coordinate. ATLAS-X partitions base infrastructure across an Uber H3 discrete global grid (Resolution 7, edge length ~1.22 km, centroid spacing ~2.10 km):

  • Zone 1: Dedicated Landing & Ascent Pad (H_pad)
    • Location & Buffer: Centroid offset 2.30 km from the habitat core behind natural terrain berms.
    • Operational Mitigation: Dedicated blast berm eliminates supersonic plume ejecta (500 to 1,500 m/s) from sandblasting crew habitats and solar arrays.
    • Location & Buffer: Positioned in central safe terrain under 3 to 5 meters of regolith overburden or within intact basaltic lava tubes.
    • Operational Mitigation: Attenuates Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR) and Solar Particle Events (SPE) to safe operational levels below 35 mSv/year.
    • Location & Buffer: Located inside polar cold traps or directly over subsurface glacial ice sheets.
    • Operational Mitigation: Minimizes rover haulage transit distance while preserving cryogenic trap integrity and preventing biological forward contamination.

Spatial triad layout in Uber H3 Resolution 7 cells, demonstrating blast wave isolation between the rocket landing pad (H_pad) and the radiation-shielded habitat core (H_hab).

Innovation 3: Temporal Power Sizing & Lunar Night Survival

  • The Polar Night Bottleneck: Orbital obliquity at lunar crater rims creates continuous shadow periods up to 102.5 hours (4.3 Earth days). Maintaining a continuous 25 kWe habitat life-support baseload requires 2,562.5 kWh of stored energy.
    • Lithium-Ion Batteries (180 Wh/kg specific energy): Requires 14,236 kg of battery mass.
    • Hydrogen/Oxygen Regenerative Fuel Cells (450 Wh/kg specific energy): Requires 5,694 kg of system mass.
    • Net Mass Savings: Regenerative Fuel Cells save 8,542 kg (60.0% mass reduction) of landed launch mass.
  • Martian Global Dust Storm Resilience: At high optical depths (tau = 3.0), direct solar irradiance drops by 93.3%. ATLAS-X sizes a dual Kilopower 10 kWe Fission Surface Power (FSP) architecture (3,000 kg total) ensuring continuous, weather-independent life-support operation.

Innovation 4: COSPAR Planetary Protection & Operational Zoning

  • Lunar Cold Traps (Category II vs. Category II*): Enforces organic carbon and propulsion exhaust accounting for polar shadowed regions to protect delicate prebiotic records under NASA NPR 8715.24.
  • Martian Special Regions (Category IVb / IVc): Identifies accessible subsurface ice deposits and mandates sterile robotic drill barriers (<0.03 bacterial endospores/m^2) alongside a 500-meter to 1-kilometer standoff buffer between human living quarters and extraction sites to prevent forward biological contamination.

What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

Our systems engineering framework evaluated six primary technical constraints:

  1. Lander Touchdown Dynamics: Spacecraft tip-over limits (surface slope <= 10.0 degrees at a 5-meter footpad baseline) and boulder collision hazards (rock abundance <= 5.0% from LRO Diviner and Mars THEMIS).
  2. Plume-Surface Interaction (PSI): Rocket exhaust ground scour ejecting high-velocity debris at 500 to 1,500 m/s, requiring a minimum 1.5 to 2.5 km landing pad separation behind natural topographic berms.
  3. ISRU Mechanical Traction Energetics: Rover transit energy across sloped regolith, verifying that hauling 1 metric ton of excavated water ice along a 3.2 km route consumes only 0.17 kWh (0.60 MJ) of traction energy.
  4. Martian Atmospheric Entry Mechanics: Siting bases in deep depressions (such as Hellas Basin at -7,150m elevation, 1,155 Pa air pressure) increases aerodynamic drag, saving approximately 12 metric tons of descent propellant (+45% to +60% payload gain) to offset rover surface travel distances.
  5. Cosmic Radiation Shielding: Accounting for cosmic radiation doses (73.5x Earth background on the Moon, 77.9x on Mars) and verifying that 3 to 5 meters of regolith burial or intact lava tube ceilings provide 90% radiation attenuation.
  6. Geopolitical & Diplomatic Feasibility: Classifying all 12 terrestrial analog sites into Open Field Deployment locations (permitted across international partner nations) versus Remote-Sensing Benchmarks (analyzed via open satellite telemetry) to respect international space policies.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Stack

  • Core Programming Language: Python 3.10 to 3.14 (computational engine fully verified on the Python 3.14.6 runtime).
  • Numerical & Physics Calculus: NumPy (>= 1.24.0) and SciPy (>= 1.10.0) for topographic slope calculus, Ledoit-Wolf covariance shrinkage, and Taylor series error propagation.
  • Data Engineering & Columnar Storage: SQLite 3 with Full-Text Search (FTS5), Pandas (>= 2.0.0), and PyArrow (>= 14.0.0) managing the 37-table master relational database (14.8 MB) with Snappy-compressed Apache Parquet exports.
  • Spatial Grid Indexing: Uber H3 discrete global grid system (Resolutions 6 and 7) for cross-body spatial harmonization between Earth, Moon, and Mars.
  • Automated Testing Suite: Pytest (>= 7.0.0) and Hypothesis (>= 6.0.0) executing 220 unit and property-based verification tests in 6.22 seconds.
  • Front-End & Mission Telemetry: React, Vite, Three.js, and Tailwind CSS powering the interactive 3D planetary globe and mission control telemetry dashboard.

Three-Tier Scientific Verification & NASA Standards

Every calculation in ATLAS-X is verified through a three-tier scientific audit complying with NASA software engineering standards:

  • Tier 1: Ground-Truth Geochemical Verification (Sample Simplex Distance): Uses scale-invariant Aitchison distance (d_A) in centered log-ratio (clr) compositional space to benchmark candidate sites against returned Apollo 14 breccia samples (d_A = 0.593) and Martian Shergottite meteorites (NWA 2990, d_A = 0.542), confirming mineralogical validity against specimens curated at NASA Johnson Space Center.
  • Tier 2: Monte Carlo Noise Perturbation Test (N = 1,000 Realizations): Applies Gaussian noise across all sensor measurement dimensions. Candidate base rankings maintain a 90.7% retention rate within the top 5% Pareto frontier, confirming stability against instrument calibration uncertainty.
  • Tier 3: Spatial Contiguity Verification (Local Moran's I): Evaluates spatial autocorrelation across 6-ring neighboring H3 cells, ensuring identified sites form contiguous operational testing zones (>25 square km) rather than single-pixel anomalies.
  • NASA Standards Compliance: Meets NASA NPR 7150.2D Class C software quality standards with full requirements traceability across 220 automated unit tests.

Automated verification results showing 220 passing unit tests, Monte Carlo rank stability distributions, and Aitchison geochemical simplex distance benchmarking against Apollo 14 lunar samples.

Project Benefits & Intended Impact

  • For NASA Artemis & Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS): Provides an objective, automated qualification engine for commercial landers (such as Astrobotic Griffin-1 and Intuitive Machines) and Artemis crewed sortie missions, ensuring touchdown safety while maximizing resource proximity.
  • For Human Mars Exploration Architectures: Resolves the trade-off between atmospheric entry mass efficiency and surface water ice access, identifying optimal landing corridors in Hellas Basin, Arcadia Planitia, and Jezero Crater.
  • Dual-Use Terrestrial Benefits: The physical algorithms developed for planetary screening directly benefit Earth observation: mapping hyper-arid soil degradation, monitoring fragile hydrothermal ecosystems, identifying subterranean karst hazards, and aiding remote geothermal mineral exploration.
  • Open Science Standard: 100% compliant with NASA SPD-41a scientific information policy, licensed under Apache 2.0, with open Parquet, CSV, and SQLite datasets.
